headline: Mission Complete — Open, Closed, or Filtered
message:
Monday, 12:31 PM. The engagement log had grown considerably.

45.77.180.10 — Development Server:
22/tcp open — SSH service. Service label: ssh. Fingerprinting pending.
80/tcp open — HTTP service. Service label: http. Fingerprinting pending.
443/tcp open — HTTPS service. Service label: https. Fingerprinting pending.
3306/tcp filtered — MySQL port. Probe blocked. State unknown. Follow-up required.
8080/tcp closed — HTTP-proxy port. RST received. No service listening.

45.77.180.11 — Legacy Server:
22/tcp open — SSH service. Service label: ssh. Fingerprinting pending.
80/tcp open — HTTP service. Service label: http. Fingerprinting pending.
8443/tcp open — Alternative HTTPS service. Service label: https-alt. FOUND ON FULL-RANGE SCAN ONLY. Fingerprinting pending.

James stared at that last line.

8443. Not in the default scan range. Not in the first pass. Visible only because Maya had run all 65,535 ports.

'If you'd stopped at the default scan...' he started.

'You would have filed a report saying the legacy server runs SSH and HTTP,' Maya said. She saved the output — three formats, all named clearly. 'Two open ports. Both standard. Nothing remarkable.' She pulled up the file in her text editor. 'And eight-four-four-three would have stayed invisible for the entire engagement.'

'What's on it?'

'That,' Maya said, 'is the right question. We know the port is open. We do not know what service is running, what version it is, or what it is called. The service column says https-alt — that is the IANA label for port 8443. Not confirmed.' She looked at James. 'Do you know what we do when we want to know exactly what is behind an open port?'

James thought about it. They had built the port map. They had not yet looked inside any of the open rooms.

'We fingerprint it,' he said.

'We fingerprint it.'

---

In this mission, you crossed from 'we know which hosts are alive' to 'we know which doors exist.' That is the second layer of the attack surface — not just which systems are present, but which services they are running and which ports those services sit behind.

You also learned the most important discipline in port scanning: the full-range scan. The default scan is a starting point — it finds the obvious services quickly, and for large ranges it gives you the first actionable picture. But the interesting findings — the forgotten management interfaces, the legacy endpoints, the misconfigured services — often live on ports that beginners never check.

45.77.180.11's port 8443 would have been invisible. It is not invisible now.

You have also learned that filtered is not a conclusion. It is a question. Port 3306 on the development server is filtered — which means a database might be sitting behind that firewall rule, reachable through paths the direct scan could not see. That investigation is part of what continues.

The OCF framework: Open, Closed, Filtered. Three states, three professional responses. Every port you encounter in this engagement lands in one of them — and each one tells you something different about what to do next.

The port map is built. The next question is behind every open door: what is actually running in there?

badgesUnlocked.name: Door Mapper
badgesUnlocked.description: Completed Mission 2: Open, Closed, or Filtered — built the first active port map of the Meridian Financial engagement. Correctly interpreted all three port states at the packet level, ran a full-range scan that revealed a service invisible to the default scan, recognised that filtered ports are never the same as cleared, and documented findings in a professional engagement log with accurate state labels.

nextSteps: Mission 3: What's Behind the Door — You have a port map. The service labels are IANA conventions, not confirmed identities. Mission 3 introduces service fingerprinting — the technique that probes each open port and analyses the response to determine exactly what software is running, which version, and what that version's known exposure looks like.

Optional: Return to the port scanning lab and attempt the 'hidden service' challenge — find a service running on a port that Nmap's service label does not match. This builds the instinct for treating service labels as hypotheses, not facts.
Review: The OCF framework (Open → Closed → Filtered) is your port scanning interpretation model from here forward. Open and filtered both require active follow-up. Only closed is a definitive answer.
